library(devtools) devtools::install_github(repo="nmatzke/BioGeoBEARS")

Thanks!

> library(devtools)
> devtools::install_github(repo="nmatzke/BioGeoBEARS", INSTALL_opts="--byte-compile")
>

messages.body_plain:
Hi -- this looks like it might be an issue with whether or not the null range is included in the model, vs. in the plot?  Search your script on include_null_range and make sure it matches throughout.

PS I wouldn't call it a GeoSSE model, DIVALIKE (and the other BioGeoBEARS models) can be viewed as special cases of ClaSSE models, but with lineage extinction ("E") set to 0, the birthrate (speciation=S) fixed to the Yule (pure-birth process), and with state-dependent speciation (SS) only existing in the limited sense that different kinds of cladogenesis get different weights.  See:

Matzke, Nicholas J. (2022). Statistical comparison of DEC and DEC+J is identical to comparison of two ClaSSE submodels, and is therefore valid. Journal of Biogeography, 49(10), 1805-1824. doi: 10.1111/jbi.14346

Cheers,
Nick

If you are doing a trait-dependent dispersal model, your ancestral state estimates after the ML run are the probabilities of the JOINT geography+trait states, at each node.

To get this plotted correctly, you then have to collapse the joint geog+trait ancestral state estimates into a:

(a) a geography-only ancestral state estimates results object
(b) a traits-only ancestral state estimates results object

Now (a) can be plotted like normal biogeography, and (b) can be plotted by setting include_null_range to FALSE and max_range_size to 1.

A complete example is available in the zipfile at:
http://phylo.wikidot.com/biosci-395-labs

Here is the code for extracting geog-only and trait-only ancestral states, from the joint ancestral states:

==============
#######################################################
# Extract just geography ancestral states from geog+trait ancestral states
#######################################################
geog_res = get_geog_from_traitgeog_results(res=resDECj_t12_t21_m2, num_trait_states=2)

#######################################################

#######################################################
trait_res = get_trait_from_traitgeog_results(res=resDECj_t12_t21_m2, num_trait_states=2)
tipranges = getranges_from_LagrangePHYLIP(lgdata_fn=slashslash(paste(labpt2a, "geog.data", sep="/")))

#######################################################
# Plot the geographic ancestral states
#######################################################
analysis_titletxt = "S. conifers: Geog reconstruction under DEC+J+trait"

scriptdir = np(system.file("extdata/a_scripts", package="BioGeoBEARS"))

results_object = geog_res

#######################################################
# Plot the trait ancestral states
#######################################################
analysis_titletxt = "S. conifers: Trait reconstruction under DEC+J+trait"
results_object = trait_res
res2 = plot_BioGeoBEARS_results(results_object, analysis_titletxt, addl_params=list("t12","t21"), plotwhat="text", label.offset=0.45, tipcex=0.7, statecex=0.7, splitcex=0.6, titlecex=0.8, plotsplits=TRUE, cornercoords_loc=scriptdir, include_null_range=FALSE, tr=tr, tipranges=trait_values)

Therefore, DIVALIKE with m2 = 1 or DIVALIKE m2 = 0.5 is the same since LRT is nonsignificant. So, how dare I be if I check the rate of true positive results with my simulations? What am I supposed to expect, given that both models (i.e., DIVALIKE with m2 = 1 and DIVALIKE with m2 = 0.5) are the same? A positive rate equals the P-value cutoff as the dataset size increase?

My guess is that, for 39 tips, it will be hard to detect* an effect size of m2=0.5.  In our recent papers with the trait-dependent dispersal model, it looked roughly like this in simulation-inference tests (from memory):

Effect size of m2=0.5 -- needs 150+ tips
Effect size of m2=0.125 -- needs ~50 tips
Effect size of m2=0.0 -- needs ~25 tips

This should not be surprising: stronger effects are easier to detect.

(* detect means e.g.: get a p-value <0.05 in a LRT)

Now, there is nothing magical about a p<0.05 cutoff.  You could, say, get an m2 estimate of 0.51, the LRT p-value is 0.2, and you could report that and say it's evidence for the hypothesis that the trait matters for dispersal; it's just that it is very weak evidence.  Basically the LRT is telling you that, if the null model (m2=1.0) is true, you would get an m2 estimate of 0.51 or less 20% of the time.

So, to a first approximation, the LRT p-value cutoff does not change with dataset size.  (There is probably more that could be said there, the argument for the LRT operation is an "in the limit of large data" argument, so it might be too generous with small dataset size; but it would be in the details, and anyway, adjustments would make it harder to get a statistically-significant result.

(Anecdotally, in the various simulation-inference experiments I have done, I haven't noticed any particular bias in the LRT with dataset size; these are when simulating under the actual null model and then fitting an alternative model.  A stronger argument would be that the real-life process that produced real data is always going to be much more complex than the alternative model, and that any deviation between real-life and the null model might be picked up as evidence against the null & thus interpreted as in favor of the alternative.  This (a) again means that the LRT is, if anything, being generous, so corrections would make it harder to claim statistical significance, and (b) gets us into the general philosophy of hypothesis-testing in a world where "all models are wrong". The short version is this leads me to favour AICc over LRT (although I typically do both), try to compare a bunch of models at once with AICc (6-50ish), and always acknowledge that the AICc-best model is relatively the best, but with no expectation that it is the true model, and that some future model that we haven't thought-of/programmed yet could always be a better fit.)

Cheers,
Nick

Hi!  OK, apologies again for the issues.

What has happened is that something was updated in R, such that some of the checks for different cases in the past (primarily branches with, or without anagenetic events on them) were giving invalid results (e.g. FALSE FALSE instead of just FALSE).

I have worked through both non-stratified/regular, and time-stratified, Biogeographic Stochastic Mapping, on the example dataset, and gotten both to run without those crashes.

Please:

1. Update R to latest version  (probably not required, but this is what I did)

2. Update BioGeoBEARS with:

library(devtools)
devtools::install_github(repo="nmatzke/BioGeoBEARS")

3. Restart R and try re-running your BSM script.

Cheers!
Nick

Dear Nick,
thank you for your reply and the nice explanation concerning simulations.
Now, I am trying to run my stochastic mapping script (available on your site) for a stratified analysis under DIVALIKE + j. Unfortunately, I get the following error:

Failure on stochastic mapping attempt #99/100 tries. Holding at success #0/50. [1] "Error in condprobs_Left_branch_bot %*% independent_likelihoods_on_each_branch[[i]] : \n non-conformable arguments\n" attr(,"class") [1] "try-error" attr(,"condition") <simpleError in condprobs_Left_branch_bot %*% independent_likelihoods_on_each_branch[[i]]: non-conformable arguments> Beginning stochastic mapping UPPASS (i:Leftnode,j:Rightnode,anc:Ancnode;): 3:5,4:3,anc:4; Error in condprobs_Left_branch_bot %*% independent_likelihoods_on_each_branch[[i]] : non-conformable arguments  Failure on stochastic mapping attempt #100/100 tries. Holding at success #0/50. [1] "Error in condprobs_Left_branch_bot %*% independent_likelihoods_on_each_branch[[i]] : \n non-conformable arguments\n" attr(,"class") [1] "try-error" attr(,"condition") <simpleError in condprobs_Left_branch_bot %*% independent_likelihoods_on_each_branch[[i]]: non-conformable arguments>

Such an error concerns the following section of the script:
runBSMslow = TRUE
if (runBSMslow == TRUE)
{
  # Saves to: RES_clado_events_tables.Rdata
  # Saves to: RES_ana_events_tables.Rdata
  BSM_output = runBSM(res, stochastic_mapping_inputs_list=stochastic_mapping_inputs_list, maxnum_maps_to_try=100,
                      nummaps_goal=50, maxtries_per_branch=40000, save_after_every_try=TRUE,
                      savedir=getwd(), seedval=12345, wait_before_save=0.01)

  RES_clado_events_tables = BSM_output$RES_clado_events_tables
  RES_ana_events_tables = BSM_output$RES_ana_events_tables
} else {
  # Load previously saved...

  # Loads to: RES_clado_events_tables
  load(file="RES_clado_events_tables.Rdata")
  # Loads to: RES_ana_events_tables
  load(file="RES_ana_events_tables.Rdata")
  BSM_output = NULL
  BSM_output$RES_clado_events_tables = RES_clado_events_tables
  BSM_output$RES_ana_events_tables = RES_ana_events_tables
} # END if (runBSMslow == TRUE)

Also, this part of the code gives NULL results:
# Check inputs (doesn't work the same on unconstr)
names(stochastic_mapping_inputs_list)
stochastic_mapping_inputs_list$phy2
stochastic_mapping_inputs_list$COO_weights_columnar
stochastic_mapping_inputs_list$unconstr
set.seed(seed=as.numeric(Sys.time()))

I have examined the stochastic_mapping_inputs_list and it is a list, not a data frame.
My analysis includes a trait-dependent model + changing distance over time.
Thank you again.
My best regards,
José.

Hi -- it's not weird at all.  You can even stochastically map the geography & trait separately, and then summarize across both.  Whether or not this is useful depends on e.g. the certainty of the trait reconstruction.  If you have close to 100% confidence in the trait reconstruction at the nodes of interest, stochastic mapping the trait doesn't add much.

Nick

Hi -- that is peculiar, BAYAREALIKE+J is usually very similar to the other +J models.  It's somewhat possible that the BAYAREALIKE model gets very different ML parameter estimates, and when these are used as the starting points for BAYAREALIKE+J, it takes longer to get into the right zone of parameter space.

You might consider running with the optimiser optimx instead of GenSA  -- the latter is slower & more thorough, but probably overkill for the 2/3 parameter models.

My gut feeling is your BAYAREALIKE+J has got to be just about done.  But if you decide to kill it, just survey the screen printout and write down the parameter values producing the best lnLs, you can use these as starting points in a new search...

Cheers,
Nick

Hi all,

I have made a few more updates to the Biogeographic Stochastic Mapping (BSM) code for time-stratified analyses -- it should throw a lot fewer warnings etc. now.  Much of this was improving some things messed up by R updates, and the handling of the case of fossil tips (which do not come all the way up to the present).

Get the updates from GitHub as follows:

library(devtools)
devtools::install_github(repo="nmatzke/BioGeoBEARS")

Cheers,
Nick
